I do not like the direction this game and company is traveling lately.
Elden Ring is good, duh, I won't argue with that. However, there's a lot of issues that are baffling.

The Enemies:
There's maybe... 10 or so enemies in the game, with a few area distinct enemy types. It seems that without a linear world to hinge on, Fromsoftware forgot how to design challenging encounters. Expect seemingly random enemy placements outside of the legacy dungeons and catacombs and caves.
On the topic of dungeons, what a pathetic excuse for content are the copy-pasted catacombs. If you don't enjoy spirit summons, there's practically no reason to explore defeat the boss at the end of the majority of catacombs. You get shafted out of practically a third of the game's content being exciting.
Oh, also you can parry every basic weapon wielding enemy in the game for an easy victory.

The World:
The Lands Between is... beautiful. Until you get bored of the big tree and the grass that is. There is a lot of grass and very little reason to traverse it. It seems that Fromsoftware was too afraid to place weapons and armour out in the open world except in a few specific cases, perhaps concerned people wouldn't find it. Expect to find 2 dollars and a pile of crab eggs for killing a giant bear.
Legacy dungeons. These initially solved my fear that Elden Ring would be a big empty world, the prospect of exploring actual castles dotting the landscape sounds incredible! There is one castle in the base game. There is a manor with minorly hot water dyed to look like lava, an academy with one classroom in total, a city with enough housing for maybe one thousand people, and a bunch of forts claiming to be unique.
Shoutout to Redmane Castle though, definitely the best part of the game in my opinion. Too bad most people don't even fight through it, as a certain trigger caused by playing the game deletes all of the enemies in the castle and locks the doors to treasure to give players a red carpet to fighting

[h2]TL;DR – Not Recommended (Overrated, Falling Short of Promises)[/h2]
[h3]Intro & Context[/h3]
Cyberpunk 2077 has great visuals, fun cyberware customization, and a decent ending, but it falls far short of its pre-launch promises. I often see players calling this game phenomenal, praising its side quests, build variety, combat, writing, and voice acting. Personally, I disagree on almost every front. While the game has its strengths, the gap between what was promised prior to launch and its actual execution falls short. What [i]Cyberpunk 2077[/i] could have been versus what it ended up being are a universe apart.
[h3]1. Shallow Dialogue and the Illusion of Choice[/h3]
To me, the dialogues feel shallow, and the options provided are sometimes plain stupid. For example, V’s tone will jump from a neutral voice to an angry voice and back to neutral, completely predefined by the situation. If a situation is negative and I want to play it positive or neutral, I simply can't. The dialogues are tied strictly to fixed objectives; it feels like the player has a choice, when in reality, they don't. Even when choices are made, there are no real consequences or major differences, as everything converges to the same outcome.
The game ignores player agency even in small details. Smoking and drinking are heavily forced into the story, and you often cannot refuse them. On top of that, the plot suffers from noticeable holes (or poorly explained narratives), such as the Johnny Silverhand helicopter flashback where Rogue says, "Not again," which feels jarring and unexplained.
[h3]2. Wasted Potential in Lifepaths and Narrative[/h3]
The game offers three character origins, so I naturally expected three distinct storylines. Instead, they all revolve around the exact same plot with minimal differences.
In a way, I was disappointed that I couldn't have a more unique experience. I wanted to play V as a true corporate spy. Infiltrating corporations, stealing corpo secrets, engaging in Arasaka

The gameplay teeters between mediocre jank and downright bad, but the thought of its potential pushes it forward. The promise of good writing propels me through middling side activities and decent story missions, but never quite meets expectations. Characters are believably real, but never so interesting that they cross my mind when not on screen. For every good moment there is a swamp of bad, or even just ok moments. 

The ultimate failure of 2077 is that its just kind of... ok. If you have any interest in the setting at all, you will probably enjoy the game. Rest assured, the next game Projekt Red releases will also be broken forever, and kind of good.

[b]Cyberpunk 2077[/b] has an incredible amount of potential, but I struggle to understand how such an interesting universe can feel so average in its execution. I first tried it in 2020 and disliked almost everything, from the story to the gameplay. Returning several years later, I can recognise the improvements, but many fundamental problems remain. Night City is beautiful, its architecture and visual design are impressive, and the universe has enormous potential. Unfortunately, a beautiful city filled with NPCs does not automatically become a living world.

One of my biggest problems is how superficial the world feels. Too many NPCs exist simply to fill the streets. Most stand around doing practically nothing, staring into the distance or repeating basic animations. You occasionally see characters talking, but these interactions rarely develop into anything meaningful. I am not asking for every NPC to have a complex routine or storyline. I mean basic everyday life: people interacting, recognising familiar faces, following routines and reacting naturally. Night City should feel like a place that exists independently of the player. Instead, it feels like a backdrop. Fewer NPCs with meaningful interactions would have been better than streets full of characters that barely do anything.

Other open-world games handle this better. The Witcher 3 makes Geralt feel connected to the world, with people recognising him as a mutant. Bethesda games also use conversations and NPC reactions to acknowledge the player's presence and actions. In Skyrim, even a bard singing about your achievements makes your progress feel relevant. Cyberpunk rarely creates that connection. Mission characters may know V is a mercenary, but the rest of the world barely acknowledges who you are or what you have accomplished.
